visible.summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2024 penal code criminalises homosexuality; its application to trans expression runs through the indecency provisions (Art 225) and the code's vague drafting.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 penal code application to trans expression is via indecency provisions; drafting vagueness noted by HDT.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (6 November 2024): Mali’s new penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with harsh penalties; previously legal but vague "public indecency" provisions (Article 225) were used against LGBT people and gender-nonconforming expressions, and the new law bans the undefined "promotion" of homosexuality, greatly expanding who can be prosecuted.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Mali's new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Conversation (15 January 2025), interview with anthropologist Christophe Broqua: Mali’s new penal code — announced October 2024, in force 13 December 2024 — criminalises homosexuality and any citizen seen to encourage it, a sharp escalation under the military junta alongside clampdowns on opposition and media.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Mali: official assessment - same-sex conduct not criminalised but significant societal stigma; violence and instability from armed groups.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Mali: documents gender inequality, FGM, corruption, and 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' among other human-rights problems.

visible.summary:
Burkina Faso is dangerous for trans visitors. In July 2024 the military junta approved a revised Personal and Family Code criminalising homosexuality — Burkina Faso had never previously outlawed it. The junta (Traoré) has clamped down on opposition and media, promised elections have not been held, and much of the country faces jihadist insurgency. Enforcement details of the new law remain unclear (HDT notes drafting uncertainty), but the direction and the absence of any institutional recourse are unambiguous.

For a visitor: new criminalisation under a junta, plus severe general security conditions.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2024 family-code criminalisation targets homosexuality — trans people are captured via birth-sex legal status and the law's broad drafting.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 family-code criminalisation is new; enforcement practice not yet documented.

sources.claim: BBC (11 July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta announced a ban on homosexual acts — homosexuality had never before been outlawed in the socially conservative West African state; part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage/family law. SUPERSEDED: the ban entered into force as criminal-code law on 1 Sep 2025. For this record: the decisive policy-reversal date, later confirmed in force.

Africanews (11 Jul 2024, updated 13 Aug 2024): the junta's council approved a decree for a new Personal and Family Code (CPF) that 'enshrines the ban on homosexuality', per a presidency statement, joining the ~22 of 54 African states disallowing same-sex relations. SUPERSEDED: entered into force 1 Sep 2025. For this record: legislative vehicle and date for the criminalisation.

Human Rights Watch (3 Sep 2025): the Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the law on 1 September 2025 making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence — two to five years' imprisonment plus fines — enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space. For this record: the operative criminalisation date and penalties; core current-state evidence.

LGBTQ Nation (Sep 2025): the junta unanimously passed the law; Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala states prison 'between two and five years as well as fines' for perpetrators of 'homosexual or similar practices', and that foreigners will be DEPORTED under the law; junta rule since Sep 2022. For this record: penalties plus explicit deportation exposure for foreign nationals — directly visitor-relevant.

visible.summary:
Mozambique demands real caution from trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside Maputo is significant, and the Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the north.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2015 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: No LGR and no SOGI hate-crime statute — resident-facing gaps.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Cabo Delgado insurgency is a general risk; LGR absence is resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright International (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the 2015 penal code; no legal gender recognition procedure exists; societal attitudes broadly neutral but LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and employment/education barriers; the 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations then disappointed. Freshness confirmed: the new 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection that had existed.

GlobalGayz archive (2006-2011): dated milestones — first newspaper article arguing gay rights (Agencia de Informacao, 7 July 2006), Maputo men petitioning parliament, the LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, refugee deaths en route to South Africa; documents early organising under the colonial-era law.
Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2016) from Afrobarometer: Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant — 56% would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour (vs Uganda/Burkina Faso/Niger at 5%).

Global Voices (28 Nov 2017): after a decade of blocked applications (since 2008), the Constitutional Council — supreme court equivalent — ruled Lambda Mozambique's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration of the country's only LGBT organisation.

Guardian (30 June 2015): Mozambique's new penal code erased the colonial 'vices against nature' provision; Lambda (not yet officially registered at the time) pivoted to anti-discrimination lobbying; Lambda's Carina Capitine: the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination.

visible.summary: Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct is decriminalised and sexual-orientation discrimination prohibited — of direct concern mainly to trans visitors who have relationships or are perceived as same-sex-active while travelling.
visible.localsOnly: Trans people have no legal gender recognition; the implementation gap (health, education, employment discrimination, under-investigated violence) falls on residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Statutory protections vs implementation gap documented by Angolan CSOs.

sources.claim: Shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter, submitted for the African Commission's 81st session (Oct-Nov 2024, Banjul) by Angolan organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA, Diversidade Masculina and others) with ILGA/Synergia support: documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people in Angola.

Submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights pre-session (74th, review of Angola): foregrounds the Angolan context for lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people ahead of the state's review — a formal international-review channel raising discrimination and health-access issues.

Southern Africa Litigation Centre chapter 'Transgender Rights in Angola': maps constitutional protection gaps — Article 23 does not list gender or sexual orientation as prohibited discrimination grounds — and locates identity, privacy, liberty, torture-protection and expression rights across Title II articles of the Angolan Constitution.

VICE continental overview (Oct 28, 2019): Angola singled out as having gone furthest among African reforms — not only removing the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision but also criminalising discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services; contrasts legislative drafting strategies across the continent.

BBC profile (Apr 12, 2012): kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, becomes a mainstream star at 25 in what the article describes as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour — evidence of visible trans presence alongside formal criminalisation at that time.

PinkNews (Feb 11, 2021): Angola's decriminalisation took effect on this date — the law adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era ban describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and made discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds punishable by prison.

visible.summary:
Zambia is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) with documented recent enforcement: Amnesty International's November 2024 campaign highlights Madalitso Zulu, serving a 15-year sentence with hard labour; Amnesty's 2024 regional report documents rising hostility in Zambia. There is no legal gender recognition, religious leaders lead anti-LGBT mobilisation, and police are perpetrators more than protectors.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest; the documented serving-sentence case shows courts impose maximum terms.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years, active enforcement) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; trans people are captured via birth-sex status and indecency provisions.

sources.claim: Amnesty International campaign story (26 Nov 2024) 'Madalitso's story': a Zambian medical professional —36, three years behind bars by Nov 2024 — imprisoned for consensual same-sex conduct; his medical expertise lost to a health system short of workers; frames individual persecution of LGBTI people in Zambia.

US State Dept 2021 Country Report, Zambia: government continued to reject recognition/protection of LGBTQI+ rights; police perpetrated violence and verbal/physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation; LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of law; advocacy groups report police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals (fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha / $30-$900); discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued.

HRW report 'Dignity Debased' (12 Jul 2016): documents forced anal examinations in at least eight countries including ZAMBIA — less frequent there than Egypt/Tunisia but prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal exams as court evidence in sodomy cases (incl. a mass trial of ~20 men); recommends worldwide ban; such exams are treated by victims as painful, degrading sexual violence.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Zambia: no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons; when police detain LGBTQI+ members they often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release; no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, but President Hichilema's 30 May statement opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults; societal violence and employment/housing/education/health discrimination continued.

visible.summary:
Zimbabwe is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2006 Criminal Law Act criminalises sodomy (up to 1 year — a lighter formal penalty than neighbours, though indecency provisions add exposure), and Amnesty's 2024 report documents shrinking civic space threatening LGBT organising (GALZ operates under pressure; its offices have been raided historically). There is no legal gender recognition, political rhetoric is hostile, and mob violence is documented — but prosecution under the sodomy law is rarer than in Zambia, and a small organised community persists openly enough to litigate.

For a visitor: statutory exposure exists but enforcement is sporadic; social hostility is the main risk.
visible.tangentialFactors: Sodomy criminalised (up to 1 year, sporadic enforcement) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; enforcement pattern is sporadic.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women (sodomy and 'acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent'). (Only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.)

Amnesty International report, 9 January 2024, index AFR 01/7533/2024: 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries'. The cached copy is only the title/index page: it fixes the report's date, scope and thesis but contains no Zimbabwe-specific passages, so it cannot carry incident-level claims — treat it as the report's existence record, not its evidence.

New Zimbabwe, 9 July 2018: the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender/non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty ('nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups'), issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor: formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Mabvurira et al., 'The politics of sexual identities in Zimbabwe: A Social Work perspective?' (Int'l Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012): homosexuals live secluded lives due to prejudice; argues homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins', tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe; social workers should promote social justice for the gay community.
Taylor & Francis (Journal of Homosexuality): academic article on homosexuality in Zimbabwe (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe) official site: voluntary membership organisation established 1990, now 4,000+ community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups, 4 resource centres. Services include legal support (explicitly including for 'sodomy' arrests), counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. For the record: documented local support infrastructure — legal aid and counselling reachable despite criminalisation, useful for an LGBTI traveller needing assistance.
